en.sup: Supplied in English. The Greek says only 'the things from them'.
Supplied in English. Our Greek text has no verb here; the Textus Receptus has ἐστίν, 'is'.

01.r: Where the seventy are to stay.

02.r: The house that first welcomes them, and no other.
02.n: A form of αὐτός, 'self', standing between the preposition and the article; so placed it means 'that very house'. The translations give 'the same', 'that' or 'that same'.

03.r: Moves on to the next instruction.

04.r: Marks the particular house already spoken of.

05.r: The household that has received them.

06.r: They are to stay on in the one house, not seek better lodging.
06.n: A present imperative, addressed to more than one person: go on staying.

07.r: Taking the food offered by the household.

09.r: Taking the drink offered by the household.

10.r: The article stands for whatever food and drink the household provides.
10.n: Greek can use the neuter plural article with a phrase, here 'from them', to mean 'the things from them'. The English 'such things as' and 'whatever' each fill out that short phrase.

11.r: Marks the household as the source of the food.
11.n: Abbott-Smith gives the root sense of this preposition as 'beside'; with the genitive it means from the side of, from, of source or origin. The translations turn the phrase into a verb: they give, they have, shall be set before you.

12.r: The people of the house that receives them.

13.r: The worker has earned what he is given.
13.n: Abbott-Smith derives the word from ἄγω in the sense 'to weigh', and gives its first sense as 'of weight, worth'. The picture is of a scale: the worker and his pay balance.

14.r: Gives the reason they may accept the household's food.

15.r: The worker in general, as a class.

16.r: Anyone who works for pay, here the messengers Jesus sends.
16.n: Abbott-Smith gives the proper sense as 'a field labourer', and lists this verse under the general sense 'a workman, labourer'.

17.r: The article; 'of' comes from the genitive case that 'worthy' takes.

18.r: The pay owed for work done; here, the food and lodging given to the messengers.
18.n: Abbott-Smith lists this verse under the proper sense, 'wages, hire', not under the general sense 'reward'. Applying a wage to board and lodging is the saying's own point, a reasonable reading of the context.

21.n: μή is the negative used with commands.

22.r: They are not to shift their lodging from one house to another.
22.n: Abbott-Smith's first sense, 'to pass over from one place to another', with this verse cited. A present imperative with μή: do not keep moving.

25.r: The house they would move to.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus adds ἐστίν, 'is', to 'the worker worthy of his wage'. It does not show in the KJV, since English needs 'is' either way; our text leaves the verb to be understood.
